extracted.intended_audience: Department of the Interior, Congress, Indian agents, and Indian Affairs policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Official annual report of the U.S. Commissioner of Indian Affairs (1880) giving nationwide metrics, policies, and recommendations on Indian education, policing, transportation, agriculture, stock, and needed legislation. Contains numeric exhibits, policy prescriptions, and operational examples for agency-level practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural and industrial progress metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative measures of Indians' progress in farming and related industries, listed in a table for 'Indians exclusive of five civilized tribes' and separately for the 'five civilized tribes'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table items enumerated explicitly: 'Number of acres broken by Indians; Number of acres cultivated; Number of bushels of wheat raised; Number of bushels of corn raised; Number of bushels of oats and barley raised; Number of bushels of vegetables raised; Number of tons of hay cut; Number of horses owned; Number of cattle owned; Number of swine owned; Number of sheep owned; Number of houses occupied; Indian houses built during the year; Indian apprentices who have been learning trades.' For the five civilized tribes a similar set (acres cultivated, bushels of wheat, corn, oats and barley, vegetables, tons of hay, bales of cotton, horses, mules, cattle, swine, sheep) is presented and used as evidence of 'progress toward civilization.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Education — schools and attendance (counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counts of educational facilities and participants used to evaluate the adequacy and reach of Indian education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly cited numbers: during the year sixty boarding and one hundred and ten day schools in operation (exclusive of the five civilized tribes), attended by over 7,000 children and taught by 338 teachers. Used to show insufficient capacity and demand for more schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education — curricular emphasis on farm and domestic work
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy criterion that farm and domestic work should occupy as prominent a place as study in Indian schools; training in manners and habits of civilized life is held equal in importance to book learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report states it is the office policy to emphasize farm and domestic work in schools and asserts that boarding schools are necessary 'to teach Indian children how to live, as well as how to read and think.' This is advanced as a central evaluative principle for designing and judging schools (examples: Carlisle, Hampton, Forest Grove).

rubrics_metrics.name: Education — boarding-school policy and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Criterion that agency policy should provide at least one good boarding-school at each agency and select the best pupils from agency schools for advanced training away from home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: boarding schools teach living skills and character; selection of 'best material' from agency schools both prepares future leaders and acts as a stimulus for others. Report documents openings of boarding schools (Forest Grove, Carlisle, Hampton) and recommends expanding boarding capacity (urges not less than $150,000 appropriation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Education — funding adequacy and per-capita cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial standard and metric for evaluating educational provision: minimum per-capita cost and sufficiency of appropriations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement that, exclusive of rations, cost of clothing, books, and instruction in an agency boarding-school cannot possibly fall below $60 per capita per annum. The current appropriation of $75,000 is described as barely sufficient to continue existing work; the report urges appropriations of at least $150,000 to expand boarding-school capacity. Implication: budget shortfalls directly limit enrollment and school quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education — health screening for boarding admissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Admission health standard: careful physical examination required; only applicants certified by a physician as 'absolutely healthy' are to be accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification: earlier deaths at Carlisle and Hampton resulted from diseases contracted before arrival; the report notes current practice of rigorous physical examinations prior to admission to reduce morbidity and mortality among pupils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial apprenticeships and vocational training
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of apprenticeships and industrial instruction (carpentry, blacksmithing, wagon-making, saddlery, tinning, shoemaking, tailoring, printing, baking, etc.) as a metric and method of civilization and self-support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Carlisle had fifty apprentices learning trades; exhibits at county fair and premiums awarded are cited as evidence of workmanship and encouragement. Vocational training is promoted as essential for practical self-support and civic integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indian police — duties and measures of effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional standard for Indian police forces: list of duties and outcome measures that demonstrate the system's practicability and value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duties enumerated include arresting wrongdoers, preventing introduction of whisky, guarding annuity payments, protecting agency property, returning truant pupils, serving as couriers/messengers, notifying agents of strangers, searching for and returning stolen property, and escorting surveying parties. Effectiveness is measured by reported arrests, suppression of outlaws, protection against trespassers and thieves, and consistent testimony in agent reports to their value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indian police — compensation, organization, and discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational and personnel standards for police forces, including recommended pay policy to ensure recruitment/retention of the best men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current statutory pay cited ($8 for officers, $5 for privates) is called inadequate; the report recommends discretionary salary authority to attract and keep good men. Organizational features (ranks, command by a white employee/deputy U.S. marshal at some agencies), uniforms, discipline (dismissal for failure to obey), and examples (Pine Ridge force composition and conduct) are given as guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportation by Indians — program design and performance metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for evaluating Indian freighting/transportation enterprises: quantity hauled, payment terms, ownership transfer model, honesty/reliability, and economic impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design: government supplies wagons and harness, Indians supply ponies; payment options offered ($1.50 per 100 lbs in cash or $1.75 per 100 lbs credit toward purchase of wagons/harness). Performance metrics cited: pounds transported (e.g., 105 wagons initially; one million pounds on one agency; eight million pounds across four agencies), resulting in government savings and transfer of wagons to Indian ownership. Qualitative measures: absolute honesty (no lost packages, no tampering) and dispatch in handling freight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of wagons and harness for farming and freighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational metric: number of wagons and harness sets furnished per agency as an indicator of support for farming and transportation activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed agency-by-agency counts are provided (total 1,555 wagons as of July 1, 1879; nearly 3,000 wagons furnished since 1875). Guidance notes harness provisioning rules (double set for farming wagon; two sets for freighting wagon) and forecasts increased future need given Indians' growing interest in farming and freighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stock cattle issuance and pastoral training
rubrics_metrics.description: Metric and standard: issuance of stock cattle and measured success in Indians' ability to care for and profit from herds as evidence of pastoral training and movement toward self-support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbers issued since July 1, 1879 are listed by agency (total issued 10,283); aggregate owned by tribes reported as 78,812 head. The report treats faithful guarding of issued stock and growth of herds as evidence that pastoral pursuits are suitable and will lead to self-supporting tribes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation needed — marriage and polygamy regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal standard/recommendation: enact law to prevent polygamy among Indians and to provide for legal marriages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report reiterates urgency of legislation to provide proper marriage laws for Indian tribes and references similar recommendations in previous reports; presented as a necessary part of improving 'welfare of the Indians.'
